calibration.subject: A one-shot, irreversible, hardware-signed (--ledger) mainnet cutover executing five coupled changes in a single differential broadcast. NOT yet broadcast. Phases 1-5 dispatch before Phase 6 runs; a mid-sequence failure leaves a partially-applied cutover on mainnet recoverable only through the hand-trimming resume runbook.
calibration.raisesSeverityFor: Defects that can fire MID-SEQUENCE (after Phases 1-5 have dispatched) or that silently disable a control the operator is relying on. This is the basis of the single upgrade in this set (F-06).
calibration.lowersSeverityFor: Anything requiring the owner to knowingly do something odd. Law 3: the owner is trusted for KNOWING actions; only NON-OBVIOUS footguns are in scope. F-03 and F-05 clear the footgun test and are graded as operational hazards, not suppressed as reckless-admin noise; neither is inflated on cutover-stakes grounds because neither fires mid-sequence.
antiInflationRails: No finding in this set puts assets at direct risk of theft or loss, so NONE reaches High. There is no attacker in any of the six attack paths — every path is an operator/maintainer hazard or a detection gap. Asserting High here would be overstatement and a rejection criterion.

The DONATION under-funding in F-01 is externally-derived yield routed onto protocol-owned pots (project memory: externally-derived yield is opportunity cost, not economic loss). Under-funding a nudge pot is a marketing/allocation miss, NEVER filed as a value leak. This is why F-01 is not argued up to Medium on a value-leak theory.

F-04's dangerous path is reachable only from code that does not exist. C4 explicitly invalidates 'speculation on future code without demonstrated root cause'; grading it on the hazard that exists TODAY yields QA, and the mitigation is carried so the hardening is still cheap to land.

classifiedFindings.title: _loadSnapshotUsers does not verify the snapshot's address set against the addresses Phase 0 asserts on

classification.assetImpact: No assets are stolen and no user stake is lost — the migration path is fail-CLOSED, so a wrong user list can never produce a silently bad migration. What is impacted is the AVAILABILITY and integrity of the live protocol's configuration: the failure lands as a revert INSIDE Phase 6, after Phases 1-5 have already been irrevocably dispatched on a one-shot hardware-signed mainnet run. The protocol is left mid-cutover: donors converted to a live NudgeStreamer, four dispatchers redeployed and repointed, the shared BatchNFTMinter swapped for the MultiToken build and the old one retired — while the three NFTStakerDepletion instances (2 / 156 / 13 users) sit half or wholly unmigrated. Recovery is only via the hand-trimming resume runbook, which is itself the subject of four open findings on this ledger (L-02/L-03/L-07 and F-03 in this set).
attackPath: 1. No attacker is required. The precondition is an operational one: `npm run promotion-ready:snapshot` is re-run before the broadcast (the runbook requires a fresh list; L-07 flags staleness for the same reason).

2. scripts/snapshot-depletion-stakers.js:98-106 resolves the three staker addresses by regex `(0x[0-9a-fA-F]{40})` over server/deployments/mainnet-addresses.ts. That regex accepts a `0x000…0` 'not deployed' placeholder as a valid match, and this project has ALREADY produced exactly that state: deploy records carried zero placeholders for three LIVE, funded NFTStakerDepletion instances (recorded in project memory as the mainnet-addresses stale trap).
3. The snapshot is written targeting a wrong, zero, or superseded staker address. Its `.stakers.<key>.address` field records the address it actually used — but nothing ever reads that field.
4. Phase 0 asserts on the script's own V1_STAKER_EYE/SCX/FLX constants and passes. It never opens the snapshot file, so the mismatch is invisible pre-broadcast.
5. Phases 1-5 dispatch: NudgeStreamer live, four donor dispatchers redeployed, BatchNFTMinterMultiToken swapped in, old batch minter retired.
6. Phase 6 calls _loadSnapshotUsers, which reads ONLY `.stakers.<key>.users`. The list is empty or wrong for the staker actually being migrated.

7. The run reverts inside _migrateStaker — at DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol:1549 ('snapshot user list is empty but V1 still holds stake') for the empty case, or at :1552 ('V1 still holds stake after migrate - widen the snapshot and re-run') / :1553 (conservation) for the partial case.

8. Outcome: a partially-applied, irreversible mainnet cutover. The Ledger session must be re-established, the progress file hand-trimmed, and the resume leg driven — with every resume-path hazard on this ledger now in the live blast radius.
classification.likelihood: medium. It needs no attacker and no owner malice, only a mis-resolved snapshot address — a condition this project has demonstrably produced before on these exact three contracts. It is bounded downward by the fact that the CURRENT snapshot file is correct (all three `.address` fields verified equal to the script constants), so the defect fires only if the snapshot is regenerated into a bad state before the broadcast.
classification.assumptions: (1) The snapshot is regenerated before the broadcast rather than the verified-good current file being reused. (2) resolveAddress picks up a zero placeholder or a superseded address from server/deployments/mainnet-addresses.ts.
classification.externalRequirements: The off-chain state file server/deployments/mainnet-addresses.ts must be stale or carry a zero placeholder at snapshot time. This is external to the Solidity, and is the documented realized failure mode on this project — it is a stated external requirement, not a hand-wavy hypothetical.

classifiedFindings.justification: Upgraded to Medium, and the upgrade rests entirely on WHEN the guard fires, not on any new claim about what it catches. The finding is NOT that a bad migration slips through — it cannot; the code is fail-closed and that is stated plainly. The finding is that the only guard sits at :1549/:1552-1553, deep inside Phase 6, whereas its cost could be paid for by a single `require` in Phase 0 comparing the snapshot's own recorded `.address` fields against V1_STAKER_EYE/SCX/FLX. On a repeatable script this is a Low: you re-run it. On a one-shot, irreversible, hardware-signed mainnet cutover, converting an atomic pre-broadcast abort into a mid-sequence revert IS the impact — 'the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted' is met squarely, with the assumption and external requirement both stated and both historically realized. This is precisely the discriminator the deduplicator used to refuse the collapse into L-07: L-07's own recorded impact is 'atomic, before a single transaction is broadcast', which is why L-07 is correctly a Low and why F-06 is not. Medium and no higher: no assets are at direct risk, nothing is stolen, and the fail-closed rails hold, so the High bar is not approached.
classifiedFindings.recommendation: Add a Phase 0 snapshot-provenance probe, before any mutation, that requires `.stakers.<key>.address == V1_STAKER_<X>` for all three stakers and `.chainId == 1`. This is the finding's whole fix and costs three string comparisons on a file Phase 0 must open anyway. Separately, harden scripts/snapshot-depletion-stakers.js:98-106's resolveAddress() to reject the zero address explicitly rather than accepting `0x000…0` as a valid 40-hex match — that closes the realized upstream cause rather than only detecting it downstream. NOTE for the fix author: the file-EXISTENCE probe and the `.blockNumber` freshness assertion belong to open ledger entry L-07 (b28492ce…) per scope-narrowing SN-23-01, and should land in the same Phase 0 block; they are cited here so the operator implements one probe, not two.

evidenceCorrection.severity: MUST be applied by the report-writer
evidenceCorrection.wrong: The finding text cites `:1681-1682` as the fail-closed guard.
evidenceCorrection.correct: The Phase 6 guards are DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol:1549 (empty-list) and :1552-1553 (post-migrate totalStaked + conservation), inside _migrateStaker. The Phase 7 backstop is :1697-1699 (`V1 EYE/SCX/FLX still holds stake`).
evidenceCorrection.whatIsActuallyAt1681To1682: Pauser-registry membership checks (`!Pauser(PAUSER).isRegistered(V1_STAKER_*)`) — unrelated to the migration guard.

evidenceCorrection.impactOnSeverity: None. The correction moves the guard EARLIER within the same phase and confirms the mid-sequence framing the Medium rests on.

classifiedFindings.title: Phase 8's _probePoolerDonation — the mechanised form of story-072 checklist line 1197 — is reachable only under `if (isPreview)`, so the broadcast path never runs it

classification.assetImpact: None directly. If BalancerPoolerV2._psmDonate were to fail after the cutover, the try/catch swallows it and the index-4 mint still succeeds — the consequence is that a donation which should have reached the batch minter's nudge pot is skipped. Per this project's standing position, those pots are funded by externally-derived yield on protocol-owned capital, so an under-delivered donation is an allocation/marketing miss, NOT an economic loss and NOT a value leak. The real impact is on DETECTION: the wiring assertions cannot see it, because the wiring is in fact correct, so a fully green `:verify` run coexists with a silently non-donating pooler.
attackPath: 1. No attacker. Precondition: after the cutover, some condition (a BALANCER_ROUTER or SUSDS_IS_FIRST misconfiguration — both `private immutable` with no getter, hence unassertable by Phase 0 or by `:verify` — or a Balancer-side change) makes _psmDonate revert.
2. try/catch swallows the revert. The index-4 mint transaction succeeds and emits DonationSkipped instead of BatchDonatedViaPSM.

3. `:verify` re-runs Phase 7's wiring assertions against live state. Every one passes: the dispatcher is registered, the hook is paired, the donor points at the streamer. Wiring is not the broken thing.

4. The only remaining control is story-072 checklist line 1197 — a post-broadcast HUMAN step, currently UNTICKED, which VerifyPromotionReady.s.sol:85-86 explicitly declines to discharge ('STILL A HUMAN STEP … line 1197').
5. If the operator does not perform it, the condition persists undetected. Nothing in the npm chain enforces that it happens.
classification.likelihood: low. The donation leg was empirically exercised GREEN in this session's live-fork `:dry` run against the same commit (BatchDonatedViaPSM=true, DonationSkipped=false, USDC stream-buffer delta 2485691), so the pooler is not broken today. The residual is that no automated gate would notice if it broke.
classification.assumptions: A post-cutover donation failure occurs at all — for which there is currently no evidence.
classification.externalRequirements: Either an operator omission of the manual step, or a Balancer/PSM-side change after the cutover.

classifiedFindings.justification: Ratified at Low after the Medium case was tested and rejected. The Medium case would be 'protocol function impacted': donations silently stop. It fails on two counts. First, there is no demonstrated impairment — the mechanism was proven working on a live fork at this exact commit, so the finding is about a missing DETECTOR, not a broken function; grading a working path as an impaired one would be overstatement. Second, the thing that would be under-delivered is externally-derived yield onto a protocol-owned pot, which this project does not treat as a value leak in either direction. What makes the finding genuinely reportable — and materially stronger than its class sibling L-04 — is the demonstration that the human step is MECHANIZABLE and ALREADY IMPLEMENTED: _probePoolerDonation performs exactly the assertion line 1197 describes, and it passed. An automatable, already-written, already-passing check was left behind an `if (isPreview)` gate while the acceptance criterion it discharges sits unticked. That is a real control-coverage gap and a genuine story-072 deviation, but its honest weight is Low. Consistency check: run-22 graded L-04 — the same BlockingProbeGatedToPreviewOnly family — as Low, and nothing here justifies departing from that.
classifiedFindings.recommendation: Add a `promotion-ready:verify-mint` npm key that runs the existing Phase 8 pooler probe in PREVIEW_MODE against LIVE POST-cutover state: prank OWNER, trigger one index-4 mint, and `require` that BatchDonatedViaPSM fired and DonationSkipped did not. It needs no broadcast and no signing, so it chains after `:verify` with the same `&&` discipline, converting line 1197 from an unenforced human step into a fail-closed gate. Until that ships, tick line 1197 explicitly before disconnecting the Ledger. Secondary: expose BALANCER_ROUTER and SUSDS_IS_FIRST via public getters so Phase 0 and `:verify` can assert them at all.

specConformance.criterion: checklist line 1197 — post-broadcast human check: trigger one index-4 mint and assert BatchDonatedViaPSM fired.
specConformance.state: UNTICKED. One of only two unticked rows in a 46-item checklist (44 ticked).
specConformance.deviation: The suite ships without discharging an acceptance criterion it is mechanically capable of discharging, and the story-075 verifier built to close the verification gap explicitly declines this row in its own epilogue.

classifiedFindings.classSiblingDisclosure: Same family as open ledger entry L-04 (e6f32c47…, Low, open). NOT a duplicate and NOT merged: L-04's probe is a PREFLIGHT that must move EARLIER on the broadcast path (ahead of the Kendu whitelist write); this one is a POST-MINT VERIFICATION that must move LATER, into a post-broadcast read-only leg. Neither fix delivers the other. Flag L-04-23-01 is noted: L-04's own probe ran green this session (sent == received == credited == 1e24), which de-risks L-04 without fixing it — that is L-04's re-weighing at /ledger, not a change to this finding.

classifiedFindings.title: Phase 0's expected-value literal is hardcoded into a control the runbook presents as a manual human check, and is both stale and structurally incomplete

classification.assetImpact: None directly — and this is load-bearing for the grade. The CODE is unaffected: Phase 0 derives the BPT baseline live (bptAtPhase0 == the measured 16867526417628291567945), no assertion references the stale literal, and the 16,338.819e18 figure survives only as a self-contained fixture in test/BptBaselinePersistence.t.sol:96. The degraded asset is a COMPENSATING HUMAN CONTROL: story-072 checklist line 1195, one of the two unticked rows, and the row the operator is meant to use for the post-cutover state that :verify cannot mechanise.
attackPath: 1. No attacker. The operator completes the broadcast and turns to checklist line 1195 to confirm the end state by hand.
2. Line 1195 says 'the new pooler holds the full 16,338.8190 BPT'. The live measurement is 16,867.5264 BPT. Mismatch #1.

3. Line 1195 says 'the rescued ~349 USDC (98.04 + 250.77)' sits in the streamer buffer. The measured buffer is 530.761796 USDC, and it decomposes as 99.224124 (old batch minter) + 380.000000 (DelayRelease) + 51.537672 (UniboostSCX residual prime) — a THIRD component the checklist never names at all. Mismatch #2, and it is structural, not arithmetic: the control does not know what it is counting.

4a. Benign branch: the operator treats the mismatch as a real failure and raises an alarm on a healthy cutover. Because line 1195 is a POST-broadcast row, this causes confusion and delay, not a partial application.

4b. Dangerous branch: the operator reconciles the mismatch as 'the checklist numbers are always a bit off', and the control is now calibrated to be waved through — so a GENUINE BPT shortfall or a missing buffer component on the day reads exactly like the noise they have been trained to ignore.

5. The BPT half of line 1195 is partially backstopped: :verify consumes story-074's persisted baseline and re-runs the Phase 7 conservation assertion. The USDC-buffer half is NOT backstopped by anything — and that is precisely the half whose decomposition is structurally incomplete.
classification.likelihood: certain to trigger (every quoted figure mismatches at cutover time), but the harmful branch (4b) requires the coincidence of operator numbness AND an independent real failure.
classification.assumptions: The operator actually performs line 1195 — it is currently unticked, so this is not guaranteed either way.
classification.externalRequirements: For material harm, an independent genuine shortfall must occur at the same time as the numbness. Alone, this finding causes only a false alarm.

classifiedFindings.justification: Ratified at Low, having re-weighed it as structurally incomplete rather than merely stale — the deduplicator is right that this strengthens the finding, and it is reflected in the write-up rather than in the number. This is a Law-3 footgun and it is in scope: a competent, non-malicious operator would be surprised to find every figure in a control they were told to rely on mismatching, and the surprise pushes in a dangerous direction. It is NOT reckless-admin noise and NOT a documentation carve-out — the 'documentation/style' exclusion covers NatSpec, formatting and pragmas, whereas here the degraded artefact IS the control. But the honest ceiling is Low. The code is correct and derives everything live; the primary quantity (BPT) is independently re-checked by :verify against a write-once persisted baseline; and material harm needs a compounding conditional — numbness AND a simultaneous real shortfall. The false-alarm direction, which is the branch certain to occur, cannot leave a partially-applied cutover because line 1195 is post-broadcast: by the time the operator reads it, everything has already landed. Medium would require a function or availability impact this cannot produce on its own, so Medium would be overstatement.
classifiedFindings.recommendation: Stop hardcoding balances in the human checklist. Rewrite line 1195 to say: 'confirm the new pooler's BPT equals the `BPT cutover baseline` printed by Phase 0 of the immediately preceding `:dry` run, and the streamer buffer equals its final `collectNudge -> stream buffer now` figure' — the script already prints both, under a '--- stranded value (live) ---' header built for exactly this purpose. Additionally, have `_printSummary()` emit a copy-paste 'POST-BROADCAST HUMAN CHECKLIST' block with the live-derived expected values filled in, so the operator compares against measurements taken minutes earlier rather than against prose written weeks earlier. When rewriting, enumerate ALL THREE buffer components (old batch minter / DelayRelease / UniboostSCX residual prime) or, better, quote only the total the script prints — a control that names two of three sources will drift again the moment a fourth donor appears.

specConformance.criterion: checklist line 1195 — post-broadcast human check: on-chain confirmation of the whole end state.
specConformance.state: UNTICKED, and its stated expected values are factually wrong against live mainnet at c4396b1 (16,338.8190 vs 16,867.5264 BPT; ~349 USDC vs 530.761796 USDC across three components, one unnamed).
specConformance.deviation: The story asserts an end state that does not match the state its own suite produces. This is a deviation in the story text itself, not in the implementation — the code is faithful; the acceptance criterion is not accurate.

classifiedFindings.collapseRefusalCarried: F-01 and F-05 share the story-072 checklist as an artefact but were confirmed distinct by the deduplicator: enforceable-but-unenforced (fails silent) versus stated-but-wrong (fails noisy, then numb), with non-overlapping fixes in both directions. Kept separate here.

classifiedFindings.title: VerifyPromotionReady._loadAndValidateProgressFile trusts a progress file whose write-side entries are stamped during forge's LOCAL pass

classification.assetImpact: None. No assets, no availability, no on-chain state. The impact is diagnostic quality on the contract built to be the cutover's safety net.
attackPath: 1. No attacker. Precondition: the broadcast partially applies (a mid-sequence revert or a signing interruption).

2. Because _trackDeployment/_trackConfig call _writeProgressFileWithStatus('in_progress') on EVERY step (:2161, :2169) and run() flips it to 'completed' at :435 — all inside forge's single LOCAL pass, before transaction #1 is signed — the progress file already exists, already carries all 14 addresses, and already reads 'completed'.

3. The operator runs `:verify`. Its gate `require(_isDeployed('NudgeStreamer') && _isDeployed('BatchNFTMinter'), 'Progress file is missing core deployment records - the cutover did not complete. Resume it before verifying')` PASSES, because record presence is a pre-broadcast fact.
4. The run proceeds past a gate that told the operator the cutover completed when it did not.
5. _phase7_wiringAssertions() then runs against LIVE CHAIN STATE and fails loudly — the incompleteness IS detected, just with a worse and later message than the named gate implied.
classification.likelihood: low-to-medium as a condition (any partial broadcast triggers it), but the outcome is bounded to message quality because the real detector is intact.

classifiedFindings.justification: Low, on exactly the basis the deduplicator established and no more. This is NOT an incompleteFixOf run-22 M-01 and is not graded as one: the fix's actual detection mechanism, _phase7_wiringAssertions() against live chain state, works and fires. The defect is confined to one require whose message claims a post-broadcast guarantee it structurally cannot provide — so an operator reading 'the cutover did not complete' as the thing that would have stopped them is misinformed about which control is protecting them. That earns Low rather than QA for two reasons: it sits inside the safety-net contract itself, where a guard overstating its own coverage is worse than elsewhere (project memory: falsely-exhaustive self-certification RAISES severity rather than sanitizing), and it is the SEVENTH consumer of the ForgeLocalPassPrecedesBroadcast idiom flagged in run-22's MR-22-01 recall gap — which the project's own package.json:289 documents in its own words as 'after a crash IT LIES'. A defect the project has written down and then re-instantiated inside its own safety net is a systemic signal, not a nit. It does not reach Medium: nothing is lost, nothing becomes unavailable, and the incomplete cutover is still caught.
classifiedFindings.recommendation: Make the gate read something only DISPATCH can produce. Preferred: have the verifier require `deploymentStatus == 'completed'` AND independently confirm on-chain code at the recorded NudgeStreamer and BatchNFTMinter addresses (`addr.code.length > 0`). That costs two staticcalls and turns the guard honest, because bytecode at a recorded address cannot exist unless a transaction actually landed. Alternative: drop the misleading require entirely and let Phase 7 be the sole authority, with a comment explaining why a pre-dispatch record check is impossible. Do NOT leave the current wording in place with a comment — the message is what misleads.
classifiedFindings.recallGapDisclosure: MR-22-01 (run-22 cross-run recall gap) counted six users of the _writeProgressFileWithStatus local-pass idiom across the mainnet cutover scripts. This is the seventh, and the first inside a contract introduced specifically to close a verification gap. Recorded so the gap is not narrowed by omission — it widened. The report-writer should carry this sentence.
classifiedFindings.classSiblingDisclosure: Same family as open ledger entry L-03 (ea648ec5…, Low, open) but not a duplicate: L-03's gate reads the `deploymentStatus` STRING from JS with an off-chain blast radius, while this finding establishes that the verifier never reads `deploymentStatus` AT ALL and gates on record PRESENCE instead. The two gates share no input and neither accepted fix touches the other. NOTE for the report-writer: recommendation option (a) here WOULD start reading `deploymentStatus`, so if L-03's accepted fix (restate the header honestly) lands first, the two must be sequenced — fix L-03's header semantics before making this verifier depend on that string.

classifiedFindings.title: The persisted `baselines.bptAtCutover` carries no provenance binding, so a hand-edited digit is accepted as the write-once baseline

classification.assetImpact: Indirect and detection-only. The BPT position itself (16,867.5264 BPT — the largest single item in the cutover) is MOVED by code, not by the baseline; the baseline only decides how large a shortfall the Phase 7 conservation assertion will notice. A downward-corrupted baseline under-detects a shortfall by exactly the delta. No value is moved, lost, or made unavailable by this finding alone.
attackPath: 1. No attacker, and no malicious owner. The operator is on a RESUME leg, where the runbook MANDATES hand-editing the progress file — so the operator's hand is already in the file by design.

2. The runbook's rule is 'TRIM THE contracts BLOCK ONLY, NEVER the top-level baselines block'. Deletion of the baselines block is enforced by two independent aborts (:564, and :571 / verifier :151 on zero).
3. But the VALUE is unguarded: there is no chainId, no block number, no run id, no checksum on the `baselines` object. _parseBaselines (:2013-2020) accepts any non-zero decimal string.
4. A slip that mangles a digit downward (rather than deleting the block) is adopted verbatim.
5. On a resume leg the live read of the emptied old pooler is 0, so `bptAtPhase0 = max(persisted, 0) = persisted`. The monotonic floor cannot rescue the value; the corrupted number IS the floor.
6. Phase 7's conservation assertion `balanceOf(newPooler) >= bptAtPhase0` (:1725) now passes against a lowered bar, and a genuine BPT shortfall up to the delta goes unflagged.
classification.likelihood: low. It requires digit-editing a value inside a block the runbook tells the operator not to touch — not the trimming slip the runbook actually warns about, which is already caught. Filed for recall, and graded honestly as unlikely.
classification.assumptions: A resume leg occurs AND the operator corrupts the value rather than deleting the block.
classification.externalRequirements: A genuine BPT shortfall must coincide, or the weakened assertion has nothing to fail to catch.

classifiedFindings.justification: Low. This is a Law-3 footgun and stays in scope — a competent, non-malicious operator would be surprised that the baseline is guarded against deletion by two aborts but accepts any non-zero value on trust — but it is honestly a weak one, and the classification says so rather than dressing it up. Three rails hold it down: the corruption needs an operator slip inside a block flagged do-not-touch, it only weakens DETECTION rather than causing loss, and it needs an independent real shortfall to coincide before anything is missed. Explicitly NOT inflated on story-074's conditional trigger: story-074 states 'weakening any rail re-classifies L-02 as Medium', and NO rail was weakened — four were added and one was tightened — so that trigger does not fire and was not used here. Note the shape for triage: this is a residual introduced by a fix (L-02's), which is the pattern this repo treats as more dangerous than an unfixed bug because it reads as done. That shape justifies reporting it and justifies the cheap fix; it does not justify a Medium, because the fix genuinely did what the story specified.
classifiedFindings.recommendation: Emit a sibling `baselines.bptAtCutoverBlock` (decimal string, written atomically with the value) and have BOTH Phase 0 and the verifier require it is non-zero and `<= block.number`. One key plus two requires binds the value to a block, so a hand-mangled figure no longer travels alone. Cheaper alternative if that is not worth the change: log `baselines.bptAtCutover` in human units at the top of EVERY leg and require the operator confirm it against the immediately preceding `:dry` run's Phase 0 '--- stranded value (live) ---' block. Prefer the first — the second re-introduces exactly the human-comparison weakness that F-05 documents.
classifiedFindings.triageNote: Honest low-plausibility grading is why this finding is legible rather than hidden; triage may reasonably decide to carry it. That decision belongs at /ledger, not here. It was retained through dedup and sanitization on Law-1 recall grounds with the auditor's own 'filed for recall, not because it is likely' preserved.

classifiedFindings.title: `_requireNoBroadcastFlag` asserts an invariant it structurally cannot check (cheatcode string-literal scan misses inherited mutating helpers)

classification.assetImpact: None today, and the 'today' is verified rather than assumed. The verifier's complete call graph is run -> _requireNoBroadcastFlag / _loadAndValidateProgressFile / _adoptPersistedBptBaseline / _phase7_wiringAssertions / _verifyMintAuthorityInvariance / _printSummary — all view or storage-only. The closure-mapper independently confirmed that every phase function and every broadcast site in the inherited DeployMainnetPromotionReady is `internal` and uncalled from the verifier. The standalone run empirically mutated nothing (trace: vm.envOr plus a failed vm.readFile, then abort). A `:verify` run mistakenly given --broadcast is INERT, because no broadcast context is ever opened.
attackPath: 1. THE HAZARD THAT EXISTS NOW: a maintainer reads `_requireNoBroadcastFlag()` and believes the verifier rejects --broadcast. It does not; it only rejects PREVIEW_MODE (:97), as its own NatSpec admits. The maintainer's mental model of what protects the read-only leg is wrong. That is the entire present-day impact.

2. THE LATENT HAZARD (does not exist today): because `VerifyPromotionReady is DeployMainnetPromotionReady is Script, StdCheats`, the artifact retains StdCheats and the read-write ./server/deployments fs_permissions grant.

classifiedFindings.justification: Downgraded from the auditor's Low to QA, and the downgrade is the conservative reading the evidence supports. C4 QA covers 'function incorrect as to spec, issues with comments' — a guard function whose NAME asserts an invariant it cannot check is that category exactly. The second half, the substring-only guard test, is a defence-in-depth weakness on a guarantee that currently holds STRUCTURALLY rather than by the test, and its harmful branch is reachable only from code that does not exist. C4 names 'speculation on future code without demonstrated root cause' as invalid, so grading the latent branch as a live Low would be overstatement on a set where overstatement is a rejection criterion. The finding is retained and reportable — the sanitizer's noise-threshold evaluation was correct that a guard overstating its own coverage is not a style nit under this project's standing position on falsely-exhaustive self-certification — but QA is where its present impact actually sits, and the recommendation is cheap enough that a QA label costs nothing in remediation.
